description: A year of kitchen-table weather science from the National Weather Service's JetStream online weather school. Kids crush a bottle with air pressure, build two kinds of barometers, make a cloud in a jug, float eggs in sea-strength salt water, time thunder, and draw fronts on a real weather map, then finish with a short unit on climate and El Niño. Each lesson is a quick demonstration or activity with a short reading and a weather-safety tip. All of it is free online from NOAA and in the public domain, and siblings can do it together.
includes: Link to the National Weather Service JetStream lesson plan for every lesson
Matching JetStream reading pages and free printable worksheets, maps and charts
Weather-safety discussion built into many lessons
Questions with answers for every lesson

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Heavy Air
steps: Tape a blown-up balloon to each end of a yardstick and hang the stick from a string so it balances
Predict: if one end got heavier, would it go up or down?
Let the air out of one balloon (a pinprick near the knot) and watch the balance
Read the JetStream page on air pressure together
questions: After one balloon was emptied, which end of the stick dipped down, and why?
What does a barometer actually measure?
The National Weather Service calls a thunderstorm severe when its winds reach what speed, or its hail reaches what size?
answers: The end with the full balloon, because the air inside it has weight
The weight of the column of air above it (air pressure)
Winds of 58 mph or more, or hail 1 inch or larger

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A Pressing Engagement
steps: Lay a ruler on a table with about 3 inches sticking over the edge
Smooth a sheet of printer paper over the ruler and press down on the end that sticks out
Repeat with a full opened sheet of newspaper and compare
questions: Which was harder to lift, the printer paper or the newspaper? Why?
About how much does air press on each square inch at sea level?
answers: The newspaper, because little air could get underneath it, so the air pressing down on top was not balanced
About 14.7 pounds
lessons.notes: A two-minute demonstration; pair it with the next lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Going with the Flow
steps: Lay two empty soda cans on their sides about an inch apart
Predict whether blowing between them will push them apart or pull them together
Put your face near the table and blow hard between the cans; try again until they move
Talk through your family's tornado plan
questions: Did the cans move apart or together?
Which scientist's principle explains this, and what does it say?
Where should you go if a tornado warning is issued?
answers: Together
Daniel Bernoulli's: the faster air (or any fluid) moves, the lower its pressure
To a basement, safe room or interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Crunch Time
steps: Pour two cups of hot tap water into each of two empty 2-liter bottles, cover the openings and shake
Pour the water out and quickly cap only one bottle
Watch both bottles for five minutes and describe what happens
questions: Why did the capped bottle crumple?
Should you open your windows when a tornado is coming?
answers: The air inside cooled and its pressure dropped, so the higher air pressure outside pushed the bottle in
No. Leave the windows alone and take shelter inside, away from windows

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Measure the Pressure – The "Wet" Barometer
steps: Tape a ruler and a clear plastic tube inside a straight-sided glass, and half-fill the glass with colored water
Draw water partway up the tube, trap it and seal the top with clay
Record the water height and the weather at the same time every day for 5 to 10 days
questions: Who built the first barometer, and in what year?
Why did he switch from water to mercury?
answers: Evangelista Torricelli, in 1643
Mercury is about 14 times heavier than water, so the tube could be about 3 feet long instead of more than 30
lessons.notes: Construction takes 5 minutes; then keep a daily log. Run it at the same time as Lesson 6 and compare the two barometers.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measure the Pressure II – The "Dry" Barometer
steps: Stretch plastic wrap tightly over a can or jar and hold it with a rubber band
Tape a straw flat across the top so one end sits at the center and the rest sticks out like a pointer
Tape an index card behind the straw and mark where it points
Mark the straw's level and note the weather at the same time each day for 10 days
questions: What does the word "aneroid" mean?
Who built the first working aneroid barometer, and when?
When air pressure rises, what does the plastic wrap do?
answers: Without liquid (without water)
French scientist Lucien Vidie, in 1843
It is pushed in, so the pointing end of the straw rises

lessons.title: Lesson 7: AM in the PM
steps: Read the JetStream page on the layers of the atmosphere
After sunset, with a parent, tune an AM radio (a car radio works) to faint, faraway stations
Log each station's call sign, city and signal quality on the reception form
Find the cities on a map and measure how far the signals traveled

links.label: JetStream reading: Layers of the Atmosphere

questions: Which layer of the ionosphere soaks up AM signals during the day and disappears at night?
U.S. radio call signs usually start with which letter east of the Mississippi River? Which letter west of it?
answers: The D-layer
W in the east, K in the west
lessons.notes: An evening activity (30 minutes to two hours).

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Melts in Your Bag, Not in Your Hand
steps: Seal a piece of chocolate in each of two bags, labeled A and B
Hang bag A in full sun, away from walls and the ground, and put bag B in the shade
After 20 minutes compare the chocolate and explain the difference
Read the JetStream page on how heat energy moves

links.label: JetStream reading: The Transfer of Heat Energy

questions: Which way of moving heat melted the chocolate in the sun: conduction, convection or radiation?
What is the lowest SPF the lesson recommends for sunscreen?
answers: Radiation
SPF 30

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Canned Heat
steps: With an adult, paint one can flat black and one flat white, inside and out (or use a dark and a shiny container)
Put two inches of cold water in each can and check that the temperatures match
Leave both in the sun for two hours, then measure and compare

links.label: JetStream reading: The Earth-Atmosphere Energy Balance

questions: Which can's water got warmer?
What is albedo?
Why does the lesson recommend light-colored clothing on hot days?
answers: The black can's
How much a surface reflects the light that hits it
Light colors reflect heat and sunlight, which helps keep your body cooler

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Toasty Wind
steps: Ask: where does wind come from? Can a toaster make wind?
With an adult, turn on a toaster and hold a pinwheel 10 to 15 inches above it, keeping the plastic away from the heat
Turn the toaster off and explain why the pinwheel spun
Read the JetStream page on the origin of wind
questions: What made the pinwheel spin?
What is the original source of the heat that drives Earth's winds?
Finish the safety saying: "When thunder roars, ..."
answers: Air heated by the toaster rose (convection), making a breeze
The Sun
"... go indoors."

lessons.title: Lesson 11: The Shadow Knows I
steps: On a sunny day, measure and record the shadows of a few fixed objects (a post, a fence, a swing set), with the date and time
Predict whether the shadows will be longer or shorter in three months
Set a calendar reminder and measure again at the same time of day three months later
questions: What causes the seasons?
What is an analemma?
answers: The tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun (not Earth's distance from the Sun)
The figure-8 pattern the Sun traces in the sky when you note its position at the same time each day for a year
lessons.notes: A long-term project: two 5-minute measurements three months apart. Start in September or January.

lessons.title: Lesson 12: The Shadow Knows II
steps: Within two days of an equinox (around March 20 or September 22), stand a stick truly upright in level ground
At solar noon (look it up with the NOAA Solar Calculator), stretch a string from the stick's top to the end of its shadow and measure the angle
Find your latitude, multiply it by 111.1 to get your distance from the equator in kilometers, and calculate Earth's circumference
questions: Write the proportion you use to find Earth's circumference.
If your angle is 40° and you are 4,444 km from the equator, what circumference do you get?
Why must this be done near an equinox?
answers: Measured angle ÷ 360° = distance to the equator ÷ circumference
That is when the Sun is directly over the equator at solar noon
lessons.notes: Only works near the spring or fall equinox; save this lesson for then if needed.

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Water, Water Everywhere
steps: Label eight cups or jars: oceans, glaciers and icecaps, groundwater, lakes, inland seas, soil moisture, atmosphere, rivers
Fill the "oceans" jar with 1,000 mL of water to stand for all the water on Earth, and guess how much belongs in each of the others
Move the real amounts from the lesson's list with a measuring cup and eyedropper and compare them with your guesses
Read the JetStream page on the hydrologic cycle
questions: About what percent of Earth's water is in the oceans?
What is the second-largest store of water?
answers: About 97%
Glaciers and icecaps (about 2%)

lessons.title: Lesson 14: Leaf It to Me
steps: On a warm, sunny day, slip a large clear plastic bag over a leafy branch and tie it shut
Tie a small rock in the bottom corner so water collects there
After at least two hours, measure the water, then remove the bag
questions: What is transpiration?
Does wind speed up or slow down transpiration?
About how much of the moisture in the atmosphere comes from plants?
answers: Evaporation of water from inside plant leaves
Speeds it up
About 10%
lessons.notes: Takes 2–6 hours; set it up in the morning.

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Sweatin' to the Coldies
steps: Fill a glass jar with ice and cold water
Wait about 30 minutes and look at the outside of the glass
Try a plastic cup and a foam cup and compare how much water collects
questions: Where did the water on the outside of the glass come from?
What is the dew point?
answers: Water vapor in the air that cooled and condensed on the cold glass
The temperature at which water vapor in the air condenses into liquid

lessons.title: Lesson 16: The Rain Man
steps: Pour about two inches of hot water into a glass jar
Seal ice cubes in a sandwich bag and set it over the jar's mouth with one corner dipping in
Watch for drops forming and falling back, and explain each step
Talk through flash flood safety
questions: What part of the real water cycle did the ice bag stand for?
How deep must fast-moving water be to knock a person off their feet?
answers: Cold air high up where water vapor condenses into clouds and rain
Only about six inches

lessons.title: Lesson 17: What-a-Cycle
steps: Print the station cards and labels and set up water-cycle stations around the house (ocean, clouds, glacier, groundwater and so on)
Each player is a water molecule: roll a die, read the card at your station, and move or stay
Draw each move on your worksheet and play ten rolls
Compare paths: where did each molecule spend the most time?
questions: Name two different paths your water molecule took.
Did any molecule get stuck in one place for a long time? Where?
lessons.notes: Works best with two or more players; siblings can share one set of stations.

lessons.title: Lesson 18: Water Cycle Paper Craft
steps: Print the paper craft (labeled or unlabeled version) and color it
If you use the unlabeled version, add each label as you discuss that part of the cycle
Cut along the solid lines, fold on the dashed lines and tape it together, then add cotton-ball clouds
questions: Point to where evaporation, condensation and precipitation happen on your model.
Name two ways water gets back to the ocean after it falls on land.
answers: Answers will vary
Any two of: surface runoff, rivers and streams, groundwater flow

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Smoking Clouds
steps: Read the JetStream page on how clouds form
An adult puts an inch of warm water in a glass jug, shakes it, seals it with the valve stopper and pumps it up with a bicycle pump, then pops the stopper
Repeat after dropping a burning match's smoke into the jug, and compare
questions: Why did a cloud form only after smoke was added?
What happens to air's temperature when it expands?
answers: Cloud droplets need tiny particles (condensation nuclei) to form on
It cools
lessons.notes: Adult-only demonstration: matches and a pressurized glass jug.

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Head in the Clouds
steps: Cut out and assemble the CloudSpotter wheel
Compare the sky with the wheel and the NWS cloud chart, and record the main cloud type on the observation form
Observe twice a day (midday and evening) for four days, ideally around a cold front
questions: Name the four basic cloud forms.
What is fog?
answers: Cirro-form, strato-form, cumulo-form and nimbo-form
A cloud at ground level
lessons.notes: Five minutes per observation over four days.

lessons.title: Lesson 21: A 'Hole' Lot of Clouds
steps: Cut out the disc and the eleven cloud pictures and glue each picture onto its spot
Hold the disc up and look through the hole to match the clouds at each level (low, middle, high)
Record the main cloud code for each level, twice a day for five days
questions: Which low cloud always counts as the main low cloud if any of it is in the sky?
What do you record for a level that has no clouds?
answers: Cumulonimbus
A zero (0)
lessons.notes: Ten minutes per observation over five days.

lessons.title: Lesson 22: Atmospheric Collisions
steps: Point a hair dryer straight up on high (no heat needed)
Float one ping-pong ball in the airstream, then carefully add a second
Listen for the clicks as they bump, and imagine each bump joining two cloud droplets
questions: What are the two processes that grow cloud droplets into raindrops?
About how big can a raindrop get before it breaks apart?
answers: Collision and coalescence
About 10 mm (0.4 inch) across

lessons.title: Lesson 23: How Much Water Is in That Cloud?
steps: Guess how many drops of water a cotton ball can hold before it drips
Hold a cotton ball over a cup while a partner adds drops one at a time, moving the dropper around
Stop counting when water drips from the bottom, and compare with your guess

links.label: JetStream reading: Life Cycle of a Thunderstorm

questions: Why did different people get different counts?
In a real cloud, what holds the water up until it falls as rain?
answers: Drops were different sizes, cotton balls differ, and people counted differently
The thunderstorm's updraft (rising air)

lessons.title: Lesson 24: It's the "Rain," Man
steps: Make a paper ruler strip, tape it to a straight-sided jar and cover it with tape
Set the gauge in an open spot away from trees and buildings
After each rain, record the amount on the rain chart and empty the jar
Compare your totals with the official amount for your area at weather.gov
questions: To what fraction of an inch does the National Weather Service measure rain?
Why should a rain gauge be kept away from trees and buildings?
answers: Hundredths of an inch (0.01 inch)
They can block or add to the rain that falls into the gauge
lessons.notes: Build it in 30 minutes, then keep recording through the rest of the course.

units.title: Unit 5: The Ocean and the Weather

lessons.title: Lesson 25: A Funny Taste
steps: Mix one liter each of distilled water with the salt amounts in the lesson's table to match the Baltic Sea, Black Sea, ocean, Red Sea, Great Salt Lake and Dead Sea
Taste a tiny sip (a teaspoon or less) of each, from least to most salty, and find each body of water on a globe
Read the JetStream page on sea water
questions: What is the average salinity of the oceans?
If ocean water is salty, why is rain fresh?
answers: About 35 parts per thousand
Evaporation leaves the salt behind, so only fresh water rises into the clouds
lessons.notes: Taste only tiny amounts, and spit out the saltiest samples.

lessons.title: Lesson 26: We All Scream for Ice Cream
steps: Seal milk or cream, sugar and vanilla in a small zip bag
Put it inside a gallon bag half-full of ice, with a different amount of rock salt for each bag (one with none)
Shake, wearing gloves or using a towel, and time how long each takes to freeze
questions: Which bags froze first?
Does salt make ice melt faster?
answers: The ones with the most salt
No; it lowers the temperature at which water freezes and melts
lessons.notes: Great with siblings: each pair uses a different amount of salt.

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Salt 'n Lighter
steps: Fill three jars with water; stir ocean-strength salt into one and Dead-Sea-strength salt into another
Predict which eggs will float
Gently lower an egg into each jar and compare
questions: In which jars did the eggs float?
Why does salt make an egg float?
answers: The two salty jars (highest in the saltiest one)
Salt makes the water denser, so the egg weighs less than the water it pushes aside

lessons.title: Lesson 28: Diet Light
steps: Put an unopened can of regular soda and a can of diet soda in a deep container of water
Watch which floats and which sinks
Compare the nutrition labels to explain the difference
questions: Which can sank, and why?
Is warm, moist air more or less dense than cold, dry air?
answers: The regular soda, because its sugar (about 40 grams) makes it denser than water
Less dense, so it rises more easily

lessons.title: Lesson 29: How It Is Currently Done
steps: Fill a baking pan with about an inch of water and sprinkle pepper in one corner
With a stir straw at each corner, gently blow along the side of the pan to your left
Watch the pepper circle, then try blowing toward each other
Read the JetStream page on ocean circulations
questions: Which way did the pepper circle?
What pushes the ocean's surface currents?
What is a rip current?
answers: Clockwise, like Northern Hemisphere ocean currents
Wind
A strong, narrow current flowing away from shore

lessons.title: Lesson 30: That Sinking Feeling
steps: The night before, freeze ice cubes of colored fresh water and of colored salty water (two different colors)
Fill a clear bowl with tap water and let it settle
Gently drop in one cube of each kind and describe what the melting colors do
questions: Which cube's meltwater sank faster?
What makes water sink in the far North Atlantic and drive the Great Ocean Conveyor?
answers: The salty cube's
When sea ice forms it leaves salt behind, making the cold water very dense, so it sinks

lessons.title: Lesson 31: Moonlight Serenade
steps: In a dark room, take the shade off a lamp (the Sun) and push a foam ball onto a pencil (the Moon)
Hold the Moon at arm's length and turn in 45° steps, drawing what you see each time on the observation form
Switch roles and repeat, then read the JetStream page on tides
questions: What causes the Moon's phases?
At which phase can a solar eclipse happen?
answers: The Moon's orbit changes how much of its sunlit side we can see from Earth
New moon

lessons.title: Lesson 32: Updrafts in Action
steps: Float a ping-pong ball over a hair dryer on high
Tilt the dryer slowly until the ball falls out
Try two balls at once and watch them swap places
Read the JetStream page on hail
questions: What does the ping-pong ball stand for in a thunderstorm?
How does updraft strength affect hail size?
answers: A hailstone or raindrop held up by the storm's updraft
Stronger updrafts can hold up, and so grow, larger hail

lessons.title: Lesson 33: The Rumblin' Road
steps: Learn to count seconds with "one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi"
A parent flashes a flashlight, waits, then says "BOOM"; count the seconds between
Divide by 5 to get the distance in miles (or by 3 for kilometers), and repeat with different waits
Read the JetStream page on lightning safety

links.label: JetStream reading: The Sound of Thunder

questions: If you count 15 seconds from flash to thunder, how far away is the lightning?
If you can hear thunder, are you safe from lightning?
answers: About 3 miles (about 5 km)
No; you are close enough to be struck, so go indoors right away

lessons.title: Lesson 34: Drawing Conclusions
steps: Read the JetStream page on surface weather maps
Work through the pressure, temperature, dew point and pressure-change maps, drawing lines that connect equal values
On the complete plot map, mark the low, then draw the cold front in blue and the warm front in red
questions: What is a front?
Which kind of front usually brings the faster change in weather?
answers: The boundary between two air masses
A cold front
lessons.notes: About 60 minutes; print the maps ahead of time.

lessons.title: Lesson 35: Pie in the Sky
steps: Trace the North America base map and two alignment dots onto one clear salad tray
On each of the other trays, trace just one height line (contour) from the 500 mb chart
Stack the trays from the lowest contour to the highest to see the upper air in 3D
Find the ridges and troughs and the side of the trough where rain is likely
questions: What are ridges and troughs in the upper air?
On which side of a trough is rain more likely, and why?
answers: High and low places in the height of the 500 mb pressure level
The right (east) side, where air is rising
lessons.notes: You need about ten clear hinged salad trays and permanent markers.

lessons.title: Lesson 36: Quadraphonic Wind
steps: Read the JetStream page on how a tropical cyclone is built
Using Hurricane Bill's forecast advisory, draw the storm's motion arrow and its eye on the 0–170 nm chart
Plot and shade the 64-, 50- and 34-knot wind radii in each quadrant
Compare the quadrants and explain why one side reaches farther
questions: Which side of a hurricane usually has the strongest and widest winds?
How do you change knots into miles per hour?
answers: The right side of its forward motion (often the right-front quadrant)
Multiply by 1.15

lessons.title: Lesson 37: Climate vs. Weather
steps: Read the JetStream page on climate and weather
Write today's high and low temperature and compare them with what is normal for your area
Explain in your own words the Dallas/Fort Worth examples of a record rainy year and a "normal" day that wasn't
questions: What is the basic difference between weather and climate?
Climate normals are averages over how many years? Which years make up the current set?
answers: Time: weather is the conditions at one moment, and climate is the typical weather over many years
lessons.notes: This and the next three lessons are reading lessons built on JetStream topic pages.

lessons.title: Lesson 38: Climate Zones
steps: Read the JetStream page on climate zones
Make a chart of the six major zone letters (A, B, C, D, E, H) with a short description of each
Find your home on the U.S. map in the reading and name your climate zone
questions: What is the climate classification system in this lesson called?
Which letter stands for dry climates, and which for polar climates?
answers: The Köppen-Geiger system
B is dry; E is polar

lessons.title: Lesson 39: Global Atmospheric Circulations
steps: Read the JetStream page on global atmospheric circulation
Draw Earth with the three circulation cells in each hemisphere and arrows for the surface winds
Connect it back to Toasty Wind: where does warm air rise, and where does cool air sink?
questions: Name the three circulation cells in each hemisphere.
What do we call the deflection of moving air caused by Earth's rotation?
answers: Hadley cell, Ferrel cell and Polar cell
The Coriolis effect

lessons.title: Lesson 40: El Niño and La Niña
steps: Read the JetStream page on El Niño and the Southern Oscillation
Print, cut and assemble the JetStream ENSO wheel, then turn it to compare normal, El Niño and La Niña conditions
Browse NOAA's El Niño and La Niña collection and describe one way ENSO affects weather where you live

links.label: NOAA Education: El Niño and La Niña collection

questions: Air-pressure differences between which two places are used to track the Southern Oscillation?
What is La Niña?
What weather does El Niño bring to equatorial South America and to Australia?
answers: Tahiti and Darwin, Australia
The cool phase of ENSO, with cooler-than-normal water in the eastern Pacific
Heavy rain in equatorial South America; drought in parts of Australia
